_note: argv → an invocation. The declared shape decides the parse, which is the whole reason the command surface is declared: a boolean flag never consumes the next token, a repeatable flag accumulates, and a variadic positional takes the rest. Every case is (document, argv) → (command, inputs) or a typed refusal, so the binding is identical on any host that implements the corpus. The inputs map is what a declared <action> body receives as its named scope, which is why the names here are the declared names and nothing else — a body cannot reach an argument nobody declared.
document:
<cli as="tool" version="1.0.0">
  <head>
    <action as="run">return 0</action>
    <action as="one">return 0</action>
  </head>
  <command as="run" action="run">
    <flag as="project" type="string"/>
    <flag as="strict" type="boolean"/>
    <flag as="package" type="string" repeatable="true"/>
    <positional as="files" variadic="true"/>
  </command>
  <command as="one" action="one">
    <positional as="target"/>
  </command>
</cli>

cases.name: boolean-flag-never-consumes-the-next-token
cases._why: The classic argv bug: --strict app parses as strict="app" with no positional whenever the parser does not know the flag's type. The declared type is what makes this decidable.

cases.name: an-undeclared-flag-is-refused-rather-than-ignored
cases._why: Ignoring an unknown flag is how a user believes an option took effect. A CLI that silently drops --dry-run is worse than one that has no --dry-run.
